What if, in 2027, every job on Earth got done perfectly, and not one human was doing it?
Monday morning, Dave the accountant walks into work, and a laptop has already finished his whole year.
Trucks drive themselves, burgers flip themselves, and the call center is one polite server in a basement.
At first, everybody celebrates. No alarm clocks, no bosses, no meetings that could've been an email.
By week two, Dave has alphabetized his spices, then his socks, then his neighbor's socks.
By month three, people line up outside empty offices, just to feel late for something.
Then payday comes, and there's no pay.
No salaries, no shoppers, and the cash in your wallet is worth about as much as the wallet.
Wait. If machines make everything, why is everything worth nothing?
You see, money is basically a receipt for somebody's time. Like arcade tickets, it only works while the prize counter is open.
In 1930, the economist Keynes predicted we'd work fifteen hours a week by 2030, and worried the free time could give us a nervous breakdown.
So most people sink into the couch. A few pick up a brush, a guitar, or a camera, and make things nobody asked for.
Turns out, the hardest job in 2027 is having nothing to do.
Coincidence, prediction, or warning? Every prediction leads to 2027.
